problems.stem: A teacher opens TeachGen@i and types: "Plan a fractions lesson." The transcript shows a polished plan came back. Why is this scenario setup weak?
options: Fractions are too easy for a generative tool to plan.
It names a topic but no grade band, prior lesson, time block, or constraint, so the plan cannot fit a real class.
The teacher should have asked for two lessons at once.
TeachGen@i should never be used for math.
problems.explanation: A scenario the AI can usefully plan for specifies the learners and setting. A bare topic produces a generic plan no matter how polished it looks.

problems.stem: Which scenario detail is safe and useful to include when setting up a TeachGen@i prompt for a planning task?
options: "Marcus R. has an IEP for dyslexia and scored 62% on the unit test."
"About a third of the class reads two grade levels below the text, and we have no one-to-one devices."
A screenshot of the class roster with names and student IDs.
The teacher's own login credentials so the tool can pull records.
problems.explanation: Describe learner needs in de-identified, aggregate terms. Naming individual students or pasting records into a generative tool is a privacy violation, not a setup detail: FERPA (34 CFR Part 99) protects personally identifiable information in education records even when it reaches a vendor, which may use it only for school-authorized purposes, and COPPA requires stricter parental consent where students are under 13.

problems.stem: A teacher generates a plan, then realizes the period is only 40 minutes and devices are banned that day, but the plan assumes 60 minutes of laptop work. What does this reveal about the scenario setup?
options: TeachGen@i is unreliable and should not be used for planning.
The binding constraints were left out of the scenario, so the fluent plan is not usable; constraints belong in the setup first.
The teacher should accept the plan and find extra time.
The plan is fine because it was internally consistent.
problems.explanation: Hard constraints (time block, device policy, target standard) belong in the scenario before generation. A plan built on missing constraints reads well but fails in the room.

problems.stem: In a TeachGen@i prompt transcript submitted as evidence, which entry best documents a defensible scenario-setup decision?
options: "Prompt: plan a lesson. Output: looked good. Submitted."

The original scenario, the line where the teacher added the 40-minute and no-device constraints, and a note explaining a generated grouping suggestion was rejected because it assumed reading levels the class does not have.
A clean final plan with no prompt history.
A note that the teacher tried three tools and picked the fastest.
problems.explanation: A defensible transcript shows the scenario, the constraints the teacher added, and at least one rejected suggestion with the reason, so a mentor can audit the judgment.
